source.title: Proxy Compression for Language Modeling
source.authors: Lin Zheng; Xinyu Li; Qi Liu; Xiachong Feng; Lingpeng Kong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The text has some extraction/formatting artifacts, but the relevant sections, tables, and appendices are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream task performance across model sizes, which bears conceptually on V6, and includes an architecture comparison with validation BPB relevant to V4. It does not fit or test the language-model pretraining-loss power laws or compute-optimal allocation in V1–V3.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream code and natural-language task scores across models and scales, plus validation BPB in an architecture comparison. It explicitly says validation BPB comparisons across representations can be biased and focuses mainly on downstream performance. It does not fit loss-versus-parameter, token, or compute laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or estimate compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Values from cited work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: A method paper on proxy compression. It trains several model sizes only to compare input representations (tokenizer, byte, proxy), and cites Hoffmann et al. only to note that 7B/14B may be undertrained. It fits no loss-versus-scale law, makes no extrapolation, does no compute-optimal sweep and does no shape-at-fixed-size study. It reports no test of whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss. The size sweeps are comparisons of the authors' own method against baselines, not tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that mixed training on compressed and raw inputs transfers to raw-byte inference. Proxy models beat byte-level baselines under fixed compute and match or surpass tokenizer baselines at larger scales. Tokenizer and neural proxies work, gzip does not, and byte-level robustness is retained. BPB is deliberately not their primary metric.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models on mixed raw-byte and externally compressed sequences and evaluates downstream tasks; it does not reproduce the original studies’ held-out-loss scaling fits, extrapolation method, or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream results vary with model size, input representation, training horizon, and task. The paper also reports representation-dependent BPB caveats.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed 100B-symbol budget, HumanEval-Plus pass@1 for tokenizer and byte baselines rises from 0.5B to 4B, dips slightly at 7B, and rises again at 14B (Table 1). The authors note the larger models may be undertrained.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream code scores at a fixed token budget across 0.5–14B are non-monotone, consistent with undertraining of larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation BPB versus FLOPs/data for representations from BPE tokens to bits (Figure 17): coarser representations are more compute-efficient, and 1–2-bit representations underperform. No power laws are fitted.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The input representation's granularity shifts loss-versus-compute curves.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026
record.problems: Downstream task scores, rather than held-out pretraining loss, are the primary evidence for most comparisons. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the listed scores. The authors state that validation BPB is biased when comparing different data representations, and the natural-language extension tests only 1.5B models. The architecture BPB comparison is presented graphically without numerical values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row limit, omitted separate HumanEval, MBPP, MBPP-Plus and pass@10 rows from Tables 1, 2, 9, 10 and 11; robustness rows from Table 4/Figures 7 and 13–16; other representation and proxy-compressor ablations (Tables 5–6, Figures 4–6, 17–18, 22); and the late-byte-finetuning natural-language result in Appendix D.12. These do not add a distinct tested version beyond the scale comparisons represented here. Table 16’s per-task scores and aggregate rows are included.

untested.parts: No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
Text/code only, with no other modalities or regimes.
No predictive scaling of downstream scores or loss-to-task mapping.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparison.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6/V4 linking overreads a representation-comparison paper as a scaling test. The scale sweeps exist to show the proxy method's gap to baselines narrowing with size. This is a method-performance claim, not downstream predictability.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fits to held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep or fitted growth exponents.

The comparison is limited to EvaByte and OpenCoder at comparable sizes; it does not vary depth, width, or other architecture details systematically across a wide range, and the BPB values are not stated numerically in the text.
The additional natural-language experiments are still text language modeling, not other modalities or training regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The paper reports downstream scores at several scales, but does not fit a predictive scaling curve or test prediction from pretraining loss.

The paper discusses BPB comparability and training-objective differences, but does not test how fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with fitting choices, nor whether loss curves bend away from a power law.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Code-task results across the 0.5B–14B model-size sweep and the 1.5B/7B longer-horizon runs
reader_labels.reason: Scores generally rise with size, and the authors describe proxy transfer as improving with scale; see R01–R28. This is evidence of downstream scale trends, not of a fitted predictive law.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Natural-language 1.5B evaluation; and non-monotone points in code-task scale sweeps
reader_labels.reason: The natural-language results cover only one model size and show mixed relative performance; some code scores also dip between adjacent sizes. No predictive curve or loss-to-task relation is tested; see R03–R04, R08–R09, R29–R58.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: EvaByte versus OpenCoder at comparable model sizes
reader_labels.reason: The authors report lower validation BPB for EvaByte at comparable sizes, but provide no textual numeric gap and test only the two architecture families shown; the evidence cannot establish that architecture effects are only slight across a wide range. See R59–R60.
